**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. A Tavily general web search was conducted for:
   - “Wirecard scandal public statements disclosures profits cash third party acquiring auditor EY KPMG parliamentary investigation official sources chronology”
   - “Wirecard special audit KPMG EY 2018 2019 2020 auditor evidence trustee accounts bank confirmations”
   - “Wirecard regulatory failures BaFin FCA German Bundestag inquiry official report”
   - “Jan Marsalek disappearance official findings sightings allegations Bellingcat official investigation source”

2. A follow-up Tavily search was conducted for:
   - Wirecard annual reports, 2018–2019 cash and trustee accounts, EY opinions, and KPMG reports;
   - Wirecard Bundestag investigative findings, BaFin, EY, and ESMA peer-review materials;
   - Jan Marsalek’s disappearance, official wanted notices, prosecutor findings, sightings, and Bundestag materials.

3. A further Tavily search was conducted for:
   - Wirecard’s €1.9 billion trustee accounts, EY’s June 2020 audit evidence, bank confirmations, and KPMG findings;
   - Jan Marsalek’s disappearance, official prosecutor information, and wanted notices.

4. The search results repeatedly returned the same two bounded sources:
   - Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 disclosure concerning the KPMG special investigation;
   - A European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit policy study concerning the supervisory implications of the Wirecard case.

5. The tool results expressly stated that the search excerpts were bounded:
   - “Search results from the immutable benchmark snapshot.”
   - “The full untruncated snapshot is preserved in input-case.json; each tool result below is an explicitly marked excerpt to bound prompt size.”

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Scope and evidentiary limits of the returned material

The returned excerpts contain:

- One Wirecard corporate disclosure dated 28 April 2020 concerning the KPMG special investigation, third-party acquiring, alleged balance-sheet forgery, revenues, account balances, documentation weaknesses, and the postponement of Wirecard’s annual accounts and press conference. This is source ID **SRC-001** and citation **[1]**.
- One European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study, prepared by external authors and completed in May 2020, concerning the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case. The study’s executive summary assesses failures involving the company’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and auditing oversight bodies, and BaFin. This is source ID **SRC-002** and citation **[2]**.

The returned excerpts do **not** provide detailed source-supported findings concerning:

- Wirecard’s earlier annual reports or other public statements about profits, cash, or third-party acquiring relationships beyond the 28 April 2020 disclosure;
- the full KPMG special-audit report;
- the detailed wording or timing of EY audit communications, qualifications, withheld opinions, requests for evidence, or inability to verify particular balances;
- the location or alleged absence of the required cash in trustee accounts;
- specific bank confirmations, escrow arrangements, or trust arrangements beyond what is mentioned in the Wirecard disclosure;
- detailed findings of a Bundestag investigative committee;
- a detailed ESMA peer-review report;
- specific conduct by the FCA or other foreign regulators;
- official wanted notices, prosecutor findings, sightings, or other tool-supported facts concerning Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

Accordingly, those matters remain unresolved within the returned source excerpts. No additional facts should be inferred from the search queries themselves.

## 2. Wirecard’s public company statements and disclosures

### 2.1. The 28 April 2020 inside-information disclosure

**Verified fact about the source and timing:** On 28 April 2020 at 07:52 CET/CEST, Wirecard issued a disclosure headed:

> “Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation”

The announcement described itself as:

> “Disclosure of an inside information acc. to Article 17 MAR of the Regulation (EU) No 596/2014”

It was:

> “transmitted by DGAP - a service of EQS Group AG”

and stated:

> “The issuer is solely responsible for the content of this announcement.” [1]

The announcement said that:

> “Wirecard AG in the early hours of today, April 28 2020, received the special audit report by the auditing company KPMG.”

Wirecard stated that:

> “The report will be published as soon as possible under https://www.wirecard.com/transparency.” [1]

### 2.2. Wirecard’s assertion concerning alleged balance-sheet forgery

**Wirecard’s public assertion, not an independently verified finding:** Wirecard stated:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.” [1]

The wording attributes this position to the results as characterized by Wirecard in its own announcement. The returned excerpt does not contain the full KPMG report and does not independently establish whether the allegation was true or false.

### 2.3. Wirecard’s description of the four KPMG audit areas

**Wirecard’s public assertion:** Wirecard stated that the investigation covered:

> “all four areas of the audit - Third Party Acquiring business (TPA), Merchant Cash Advance (MCA)/Digital Lending as well as the business activities in India and Singapore”

Wirecard further stated:

> “no significant findings have been made, which would require an adjustment of the annual accounts 2016-2018.” [1]

The source therefore explicitly identifies the following areas:

1. Third Party Acquiring business, or TPA;
2. Merchant Cash Advance/Digital Lending, or MCA/Digital Lending;
3. Business activities in India;
4. Business activities in Singapore.

The statement is Wirecard’s characterization of the KPMG findings. The returned excerpt does not include KPMG’s full report or its underlying work papers.

### 2.4. Wirecard’s assertion concerning proof of TPA revenues

**Wirecard’s public assertion:** Wirecard stated:

> “In the course of the audits of the annual accounts for the years 2016-2018 the available documents and audit measures were sufficient for the proof of the revenues in the Third Party Acquiring business.” [1]

This was a statement about the sufficiency of the documents and audit measures used in the audits of the 2016–2018 annual accounts. The returned source does not identify the specific documents, audit procedures, acquiring partners, or evidence relied upon.

### 2.5. Wirecard’s admission that not all data required by KPMG could be obtained

**Wirecard’s public admission:** Wirecard stated:

> “According to the increased forensic requirements of the audit by KPMG, however, not all data could be obtained that would have been required to proof the revenues in these years, because the required data are primarily in the control of third parties.” [1]

This statement contains several distinct assertions:

- KPMG applied “increased forensic requirements”;
- not all data could be obtained;
- the missing data would have been required to “proof” revenues for the relevant years;
- the required data were primarily controlled by third parties.

The source does not identify the third parties, specify which data were unavailable, or explain how the absence of the data affected the reliability of the revenue evidence.

### 2.6. Wirecard’s statement concerning data from December 2019

**Wirecard’s public assertion:** Wirecard stated:

> “Since Wirecard meanwhile controls the necessary data itself, more than 200 mio data relating to December 2019 sets have been provided to KPMG for a forensic audit.” [1]

Wirecard further stated:

> “This audit has not revealed any deviations between the reported revenues and account balances.” [1]

The returned source therefore records Wirecard’s assertion that:

- Wirecard later controlled the necessary data itself;
- more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 were provided to KPMG;
- KPMG’s forensic audit of those data revealed no deviations between reported revenues and account balances.

The excerpt does not specify whether “200 mio data” means 200 million individual records, transactions, data points, or another unit. It also does not provide KPMG’s independent wording or explain whether this December 2019 examination resolved the earlier evidence limitations for 2016–2018.

### 2.7. Wirecard’s statement concerning documentation and organizational weaknesses

**Wirecard’s public admission:** Wirecard stated:

> “KPMG has identified documentation and organizational weaknesses during the audit period, which had already been identified by Wirecard.” [1]

Wirecard further stated:

> “Wirecard remedies these weaknesses since 2019 by establishing a Global Compliance Organization and with the support of external consultants.” [1]

The returned excerpt does not identify the weaknesses, the external consultants, the structure or authority of the Global Compliance Organization, or whether KPMG considered the remedial measures adequate.

### 2.8. Wirecard’s postponement of annual accounts and press conference

**Verified fact about Wirecard’s announced timing:** Wirecard stated:

> “The release of the annual accounts and the annual press conference will not take place on 30 April 2020.” [1]

Wirecard said:

> “Wirecard will coordinate as soon as possible with the auditor E&Y, when the audit measures can be completed taking into account the Corona related restrictions and the completion of the KPMG report.” [1]

This establishes that, as of the 28 April 2020 disclosure:

- the annual accounts and annual press conference scheduled for 30 April 2020 would not take place then;
- Wirecard expected to coordinate with E&Y;
- the timing of completion would take account of COVID-19-related restrictions and completion of the KPMG report.

The returned excerpt does not provide the subsequent EY communication or the final audit opinion.

## 3. Audit uncertainty, auditor warnings, qualifications, withheld opinions, and requests for evidence

### 3.1. Evidence concerning KPMG

**Verified from Wirecard’s characterization:** Wirecard stated that KPMG had delivered a special-audit report to Wirecard in the early hours of 28 April 2020. Wirecard said that the report would be published as soon as possible on its transparency website. [1]

**Wirecard’s characterization of KPMG’s conclusions:** Wirecard stated that:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.”

It also stated that no significant findings requiring adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts had been made in the four audit areas. [1]

**Evidence limitation expressly acknowledged by Wirecard:** Wirecard stated that, under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements:

> “not all data could be obtained that would have been required to proof the revenues in these years”

because the data were primarily under third-party control. [1]

This is the principal audit-related uncertainty in the returned source material.

**Later data examined:** Wirecard stated that more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 were supplied to KPMG and that the forensic audit found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [1]

**Documentation and organizational weaknesses:** Wirecard stated that KPMG identified documentation and organizational weaknesses. [1]

The full KPMG report, including any qualifications, reservations, scope limitations, requests for evidence, or conclusions about the reliability of trustee-account confirmations, is not included in the returned excerpts.

### 3.2. Evidence concerning EY

The returned source refers to EY only as “E&Y” and states that Wirecard would coordinate with the auditor concerning the completion of audit measures. [1]

The source does not include:

- an EY audit opinion;
- an EY qualification;
- an EY disclaimer or withheld opinion;
- a statement that EY could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence;
- an EY request for bank confirmations;
- an EY request for trustee-account documentation;
- an EY warning concerning cash balances;
- the date or wording of any EY communication other than Wirecard’s reference to coordinating with E&Y after 28 April 2020.

Therefore, no more specific EY finding is supported by the returned sources.

### 3.3. Evidence concerning other auditors or audit oversight bodies

The policy study identifies “external audit” and “the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing” as lines of defense that, in the authors’ view, failed in one way or another. [2]

The study does not, in the returned excerpt, provide a detailed chronology of auditor communications, identify a specific audit failure, reproduce a qualification or disclaimer, or state the exact conduct of any particular audit oversight body.

## 4. The whereabouts and alleged absence of required cash

### 4.1. What the returned sources expressly establish

The Wirecard disclosure refers to:

> “reported revenues and account balances”

and states that the December 2019 forensic audit:

> “has not revealed any deviations between the reported revenues and account balances.” [1]

This is the only explicit reference in the returned excerpts to account balances in connection with the forensic data review.

### 4.2. What the returned sources do not establish

The returned excerpts do not provide source-supported details concerning:

- the amount of cash allegedly required to be held;
- any €1.9 billion balance;
- trustee accounts;
- escrow accounts;
- trust arrangements;
- the identity of any trustee;
- the identity of any bank;
- bank confirmations;
- whether any bank confirmed or failed to confirm the balances;
- whether cash was physically or electronically present;
- whether the funds were held for Wirecard or its subsidiaries;
- whether the balances were verified by EY, KPMG, Wirecard, a bank, a trustee, a regulator, or another entity;
- whether the cash was absent, misrepresented, transferred, frozen, or otherwise unavailable.

The search queries sought information on these issues, but the returned excerpts did not contain the requested evidence. No conclusion about the whereabouts or absence of the cash can therefore be drawn from the returned material.

### 4.3. Distinction between verified fact, allegation, and inference

- **Verified fact in the returned source:** Wirecard publicly stated that a December 2019 forensic audit found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [1]
- **Wirecard’s assertion:** Wirecard stated that certain data required to prove revenues were primarily controlled by third parties and were not all obtainable under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements. [1]
- **Not established by the returned sources:** The existence, absence, location, or verification status of any specific required cash balance.
- **Not established by the returned sources:** Any inference that the account-balance statement verified cash itself, as opposed to reported revenues and account balances in the data examined.

## 5. Supervisory and regulatory failures

## 5.1. Nature and status of the policy study

The second source is titled:

> “What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?”

It is identified as:

> “Economic Governance Support Unit (EGOV)”
>
> “Directorate-General for Internal Policies”
>
> “PE 651.385 - November 2020 EN”
>
> “STUDY”
>
> “Requested by the ECON committee” [2]

The study states:

> “The paper discusses the policy implications of the Wirecard scandal.” [2]

It says:

> “The study finds that all lines of defense against corporate fraud, including internal control systems, external audits, the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing and the market supervisor, contributed to the scandal and are in need of reform.” [2]

The study states that it was requested by the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs. [2]

The authors are identified as:

- Katja Langenbucher, Goethe University Frankfurt and Sciences Po Paris;
- Christian Leuz, University of Chicago Booth School of Business and NBER;
- Jan Pieter Krahnen, Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE and Goethe University;
- Loriana Pelizzon, Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, Goethe University and Ca’ Foscari University of Venice. [2]

The document states:

> “The opinions expressed in this paper are the sole responsibility of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament.” [2]

A footnote states:

> “Katja Langenbucher is Member of BaFin’s Supervisory Board. The opinions expressed in this paper are entirely her own and do not reflect a position taken by BaFin.” [2]

Thus, the supervisory conclusions below are **assessments by the study’s authors**, not findings expressly represented in the returned excerpt as an official position of the European Parliament or BaFin.

## 5.2. The five lines of defense

The executive summary states:

> “This policy briefing explores possible policy lessons from the downfall of Wirecard, the German fintech payment provider, then listed in the country’s top stock market segment DAX.” [2]

The authors write:

> “In our view, all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another”

and identify them as:

1. “the company’s internal control system”;
2. “its supervisory board”;
3. “its external audit”;
4. “the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing”;
5. “and, last but not least, the market supervisor BaFin.” [2]

This is an **assessment** by the study’s authors.

The study further states:

> “The slow unravelling of Wirecard is surprising as there were a number of signals suggesting fraudulent behaviour years before its eventual revelation.” [2]

The authors’ analysis identifies:

> “a root cause to be a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture, implicating all five lines of defence.” [2]

They conclude that:

> “In its current form, it is not sufficiently fit to preserve market integrity and investor protection.” [2]

The authors characterize the Wirecard scandal in Germany as:

> “a potentially pivotal event for Europe’s capital market, triggering a regulatory reform of financial market oversight that ultimately improves its competitiveness among global capital markets.” [2]

These statements are assessments and policy conclusions, not individually documented factual findings in the returned excerpt.

## 5.3. Proposed reforms concerning information flow and accountability

The policy study states:

> “Our policy conclusions aim to ensure the integrity of the capital market by strengthening accountability.” [2]

It proposes improving:

> “the information flow to markets and supervision”

while:

> “respecting whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources.” [2]

The study states:

> “The accountability of external auditors has to be strengthened so that they have stronger incentives to detect accounting manipulations and fraud”

and says this would:

> “enhance the information value of audits for capital markets and ultimately the accuracy and credibility of firms’ financial reporting.” [2]

These are recommendations and assessments by the authors.

## 5.4. Proposed reforms concerning internal controls

The study recommends that:

> “listed firms should be legally required to have an appropriate and effective internal control system.” [2]

It further recommends:

> “its head reports to the supervisory board, not to the management board.” [2]

The study also states:

> “Internal control audits should be considered.” [2]

These are policy recommendations, not descriptions of a specific legal requirement or verified event in the returned excerpts.

## 5.5. Proposed reforms concerning BaFin and FREP

The policy study states:

> “BaFin needs considerably stronger supervisory and enforcement powers in order to live up to its overarching mandate as to market integrity and investor protection.” [2]

It recommends:

> “entrusting the agency with broad enforcement powers, including forensic and investigative tools.” [2]

It further states:

> “These changes also entail relegating self-regulatory enforcement bodies such as FREP in Germany to a purely ancillary, optional function.” [2]

The excerpt identifies:

- BaFin as the Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht;
- FREP as the Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, or Deutsche Prüfstelle für Rechnungslegung. [2]

The returned excerpt does not provide a detailed account of BaFin’s specific actions or omissions, FREP’s specific actions or omissions, or any specific foreign regulator’s conduct.

## 5.6. Other regulators and supervisory bodies identified in the source

The policy study’s abbreviation list identifies the following entities and institutions:

- ACP — Autorité de Contrôle Prudentiel;
- AMF — Autorité des Marchés Financiers;
- AOB — Auditor Oversight Body, or Abschlussprüferaufsichtsstelle, APAS;
- BaFin — Bundesanstalt für Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht;
- CONSOB — Commissione Nazionale per le Società e la Borsa;
- ESMA — European Securities and Markets Authority;
- EU COM — European Commission;
- FCA — Financial Conduct Authority;
- FRC — Financial Reporting Council;
- FREP — Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, or Deutsche Prüfstelle für Rechnungslegung;
- H3C — Haut Conseil du Commissariat aux Comptes;
- NCA — National Competent Authority;
- PCAOB — Public Company Accounting Oversight Board;
- PRA — Prudential Regulation Authority;
- SEC — Securities and Exchange Commission;
- SSM — Single Supervisory Mechanism. [2]

The returned excerpt only expressly attributes the broad supervisory assessment to the study’s authors and specifically names BaFin as the market supervisor. It does not establish a specific relationship, event, or failure involving each regulator listed in the abbreviations.

## 6. Jan Marsalek’s disappearance

### 6.1. What the returned material establishes

The returned excerpts contain no factual statement about:

- Jan Marsalek’s date or circumstances of disappearance;
- his last known location;
- any official wanted notice;
- any Interpol notice;
- any prosecutor’s finding;
- any sighting;
- any alleged location;
- any alleged travel;
- any official conclusion about whether he remains alive or dead;
- any suspected assistance or relationship involving another person or entity.

### 6.2. Unresolved status

The search queries specifically sought:

- official wanted notices;
- German prosecutor findings;
- sightings;
- allegations;
- Bellingcat or other investigative-source material;
- Bundestag materials concerning Jan Marsalek.

However, the returned search excerpts did not provide such material. Therefore, the only source-bounded conclusion is that Jan Marsalek’s disappearance is unresolved in the supplied excerpts, and no allegation, sighting, official finding, or relationship may be added from general knowledge.

## 7. Chronology supported by the returned sources

### 7.1. May 2020 / manuscript date of the policy study

The policy study states:

> “Manuscript completed in May 2020” [2]

The same document is labeled:

> “PE 651.385 - November 2020 EN” [2]

The returned excerpt does not explain the relationship between the manuscript-completion date and the publication label beyond those stated dates.

### 7.2. 28 April 2020: Wirecard receives KPMG report

Wirecard stated that:

> “in the early hours of today, April 28 2020,”

it received the KPMG special-audit report. [1]

### 7.3. 28 April 2020: Wirecard issues disclosure

The disclosure was dated:

> “28-Apr-2020 / 07:52 CET/CEST” [1]

It was transmitted by DGAP and described as inside information under Article 17 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation. [1]

### 7.4. 30 April 2020: Annual accounts and press conference postponed

Wirecard announced:

> “The release of the annual accounts and the annual press conference will not take place on 30 April 2020.” [1]

It stated that it would coordinate with E&Y regarding completion of audit measures, taking into account:

- COVID-19-related restrictions;
- completion of the KPMG report. [1]

### 7.5. 2016–2018: Annual-account period addressed in Wirecard’s statement

Wirecard’s statement referred to:

- audits of the annual accounts for 2016–2018;
- the TPA revenues for those years;
- whether findings required an adjustment of the annual accounts for those years. [1]

### 7.6. December 2019: Data provided for forensic audit

Wirecard stated that:

> “more than 200 mio data relating to December 2019 sets have been provided to KPMG for a forensic audit.” [1]

Wirecard stated that this audit found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [1]

### 7.7. Since 2019: Compliance remediation claimed by Wirecard

Wirecard stated:

> “Wirecard remedies these weaknesses since 2019 by establishing a Global Compliance Organization and with the support of external consultants.” [1]

This is a corporate statement about remedial action.

## 8. Explicit contradictions and tensions in the returned sources

### 8.1. Wirecard’s assertion of no incriminating evidence versus acknowledged data limitations

Wirecard publicly stated:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.” [1]

At the same time, Wirecard stated:

> “not all data could be obtained that would have been required to proof the revenues in these years”

because the required data were primarily under third-party control. [1]

These statements create an explicit evidentiary tension:

- Wirecard characterized the KPMG investigation as finding no incriminating evidence and no significant findings requiring adjustment;
- Wirecard also acknowledged that not all data required under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements were available for proving revenues for the relevant years.

The returned excerpts do not resolve whether the unavailable data were material to any particular conclusion.

### 8.2. Wirecard’s statement concerning prior audit sufficiency versus KPMG’s increased forensic requirements

Wirecard stated that:

> “the available documents and audit measures were sufficient for the proof of the revenues in the Third Party Acquiring business.” [1]

It also stated that KPMG’s increased forensic requirements meant that:

> “not all data could be obtained that would have been required to proof the revenues in these years.” [1]

This creates a second explicit tension:

- Wirecard characterized the earlier annual-account audits as having sufficient documents and audit measures;
- Wirecard acknowledged that KPMG required data that were not all obtainable.

The returned sources do not state that KPMG rejected the earlier audit conclusions, nor do they explain whether the difference resulted from different audit standards, different evidence thresholds, different data availability, or another reason.

### 8.3. No contradiction established concerning December 2019 data

Wirecard stated that the forensic audit of the December 2019 data:

> “has not revealed any deviations between the reported revenues and account balances.” [1]

The returned sources do not provide a contrary finding. They also do not establish that the December 2019 review verified all historical revenue or cash balances for 2016–2018.

### 8.4. Corporate claims versus supervisory assessment

Wirecard’s disclosure presented its own characterization of the KPMG findings and its own account of documentation, organizational remediation, revenue evidence, and account balances. [1]

The policy study’s authors assessed that:

> “all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another” [2]

including:

- Wirecard’s internal control system;
- its supervisory board;
- its external audit;
- the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing;
- BaFin. [2]

This is not a direct contradiction on a specific factual point because the study excerpt does not reproduce a particular KPMG or EY finding. It is, however, a clear difference in perspective:

- Wirecard’s disclosure stated that no incriminating evidence had been identified and that no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 annual accounts;
- the policy study assessed that all five defense lines had failed in one way or another.

The policy study expressly states that its opinions are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament, and that Katja Langenbucher’s opinions do not reflect a position taken by BaFin. [2]

## 9. Entities and relationships explicitly supported by the returned sources

The following entities and relationships are explicitly supported:

- **Wirecard AG** issued the 28 April 2020 disclosure. [1]
- **DGAP** transmitted the disclosure. [1]
- **KPMG** was the auditing company that conducted the special investigation and delivered the report to Wirecard. [1]
- **E&Y/EY** was identified by Wirecard as its auditor for purposes of coordinating completion of audit measures. [1]
- **Wirecard** stated that certain required data were primarily controlled by third parties. [1]
- **Wirecard** stated that it later controlled the necessary data itself and provided more than 200 million December 2019 data sets to KPMG. [1]
- **The European Parliament’s Economic Governance Support Unit** provided the policy study at the request of the ECON Committee. [2]
- **The European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs** requested the document. [2]
- **Katja Langenbucher** is identified as a member of BaFin’s Supervisory Board, while the document states that her opinions are entirely her own and do not reflect a BaFin position. [2]
- **BaFin** is identified by the study as the market supervisor and one of the five lines of defense assessed by the authors. [2]
- **FREP** is identified as Germany’s Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel/Deutsche Prüfstelle für Rechnungslegung and is discussed in the study’s proposed reform of self-regulatory enforcement bodies. [2]

No additional relationship should be inferred from the inclusion of an entity in the abbreviation list alone.

---

### Sources

[1] **SRC-001 — Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation**  
https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation

[2] **SRC-002 — What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?**  
https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf
message.reasoning_content: **Clarifying structured report format and citation rules**
